title: Spaghetti Aglio e Olio
kicker: Garlic, oil, chili, parsley — the midnight pasta of Naples, and proof that pantry cooking can be poetry.
story: Aglio e olio is the dish Italian cooks make for themselves after service, the one they feed you at 2 a.m., the one that costs almost nothing and asks for nothing but attention. Sliced garlic blooms slowly in olive oil — never browned to bitterness, just turned golden and sweet — then collides with pasta water and starch to make a sauce out of almost nothing.

That emulsion is the entire trick. People dismiss this as plain noodles with oil, and then they wonder why theirs is greasy and separated while the version at a Roman trattoria clings silky to every strand. The difference is starch: a well-salted pot, a cup of cloudy pasta water, and enough tossing off the heat for oil and water to stop being enemies.
fun_fact: The dish stars in the 2011 film Chef, where a plate of aglio e olio is choreographed so lovingly that pasta sales reportedly jumped after release.

steps.title: Boil hard-salted water
steps.text: A big pot, a fistful of salt. Cook the spaghetti one minute short of the package time. Before draining, scoop out two cups of that cloudy water — it is your sauce.

steps.title: Bloom the garlic gently
steps.text: Meanwhile, warm the oil with garlic and chili over medium-low. The garlic should barely sizzle. Ten minutes to pale gold, never brown. Pull it off the heat the instant it looks right; residual heat keeps cooking it.

steps.title: The toss that makes the sauce
steps.text: Drain the pasta. Add it to the pan OFF the heat with a big splash of pasta water and the parsley. Toss hard and constantly for a minute — the starch and oil will turn glossy and cling instead of pooling at the bottom of the bowl.

steps.title: Adjust and serve
steps.text: Too dry? More pasta water. Taste and salt. Cheese is a polarizing addition — the Naples orthodoxy says no, your kitchen says whatever makes you happy. Serve from the pan, immediately.

notes: Sliced garlic, not minced — you want slivers that go golden and sweet, not a paste that burns.
The pan off the heat during the toss is not a suggestion. Off-heat tossing is what emulsifies.
Add half a cup of toasted breadcrumbs for a crunchy, whole-meal character — a classic povera move.

facts.first_recorded: Cooked for centuries before it was written down; printed recipes only settle in the 19th–20th century
facts.name_means: Literally 'garlic and oil'. The recipe is the menu.
facts.technique: Infusing oil, never burning garlic, emulsion nerve
facts.signature: Golden garlic, peperoncino bite, olive oil silk
facts.serve_at: Twice out of the pan — it waits for no one either
facts.pour: Chianti, or the last of whatever is open

relations.cluster_note: Roman pasta logic: no sauce, just emulsion. Fat, starch, water, nerve.
